adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The town of Marrow Cove had always lived by the tide. For a hundred and fifty years its fortunes had risen and fallen with the herring, and when the herring left, the harbour itself became a kind of museum: ropes bleached white on the quay, a lighthouse whose lamp had been replaced by a blinking electric bulb, and a row of cottages the council had repainted in brighter colours to attract summer visitors. The visitors came, in modest numbers, and the town discovered it could survive on ice cream, boat tours and the occasional wedding photographed against the grey water.

By the spring of the third year, however, the harbour had begun to silt up again, and the fishing boats that remained could leave only on the highest tides. The council met in the old customs house and argued for an hour about dredging costs before agreeing, reluctantly, that the town needed someone to manage the harbour properly. The position had been vacant since old Tom Ferris retired, and nobody had noticed how much he had done until the invoices for the moorings stopped being paid.

An advertisement was placed in the county paper and on the noticeboard by the post office. It asked for someone with experience of small-craft moorings, a head for figures, and the patience to deal with holidaymakers who did not understand that a harbour is not a car park. Twelve people wrote in. The council formed a small committee, chaired by the vicar, to read the letters.

The letters were, by turns, hopeful, eccentric and sad. One came from a retired naval officer in Plymouth who enclosed a photograph of himself at the tiller of a yacht. One came from a young woman who had grown up in the town and had spent three years working on the ferries at a larger port down the coast. One came from a man who admitted frankly that he had never been on the water but was very good with spreadsheets. The vicar read them all twice, made notes in pencil, and then, on a wet Tuesday in April, the committee gathered in the back room of the pub to shortlist the applicants. They chose four to interview, and after the interviews they offered the post to the young woman from the ferries, whose name was Ellen Prowse. She started the following month, and by the end of that summer the moorings were paid up, the dredger had been booked, and the noticeboard by the post office carried a small, neat sign thanking everyone for their patience.
